title: Seven things your design file isn't telling your developer
description: A design file shows how a page looks. The build asks how it behaves. Seven handover gaps to close before your developer, or a tool, decides for you.
meta_description: A design file shows how a page looks. The build asks how it behaves. Seven handover gaps to close before your developer, or a tool, decides for you.
image_query: designer and developer discussing website on laptop
linkedin_intro: Tuesday is here, and so is this week's read. A design file shows how a page looks, but a website has to decide how it behaves at every size and with real content. We've listed seven questions most handovers leave unanswered, plus a simple one-page habit that keeps those decisions with the designer. Read it here:
primary_reader: Web and digital designers, and design leads, who hand designs to developers, site builders or AI prototyping tools.
creative_discipline: Web and digital experiences; design-to-development handover; accessibility and responsive behaviour.
platform: None specific. WCAG (W3C) and MDN are cited as references only.
central_question: What does a static design file fail to communicate about how a website should behave, and who ends up making those decisions?
why_readers_care: Handover gaps cause back-and-forth, rework and inconsistent builds. As building becomes faster and more automated, unanswered questions get resolved silently by defaults.
interesting_detail: WCAG requires text to resize to 200 per cent without loss of content or functionality, and browsers can detect a user's reduced-motion preference. Both are behaviours a static mock-up cannot show.
central_argument: A design file answers "how does it look?", but the build has to answer "how does it behave?" Every unanswered behaviour question still gets decided by someone or something. The more automated the build, the more likely those decisions are made by default and go unnoticed.
format: The useful discovery / workflow checklist, delivered in this week's numbered-list shape.
takeaway: Add a one-page "behaviour" sheet to every handover covering in-between sizes, problem content, empty/loading/error states, focus, text resizing, contrast over imagery and motion. Test it by checking whether a developer could answer each point without messaging the designer.
availability: None. The piece is evergreen and not dependent on any product release.
qualifications: The claim that site builders and AI tools increasingly turn layouts into code, and that this makes undocumented decisions more likely to default silently, is framed as interpretation rather than measured fact. "Rarely suits" (default focus outline) and "often the first thing to clip" are editorial judgements.
limitations: No live research tools were available this run. The supplied headlines (Zoom Slides, Copilot in PowerPoint, Claude Design, Claude Docs and Slides) all concern presentations. They were deliberately not used because the previous three posts were all about presentations and brand standards, and the brief limits a discipline to two consecutive posts without a significant justifying development. Cited W3C and MDN URLs are long-standing reference pages but were not live-checked in this run, so a link check before publishing is recommended. No customer questions were supplied.
history_summary: Numbered-list article on design-to-development handover for web designers. Argument: a design file shows how a page looks, but a website must decide how it behaves, and unanswered behaviour questions get decided by default, increasingly silently as building becomes automated. The seven gaps covered are in-between screen sizes, problem content, empty/loading/error states, keyboard focus, 200 per cent text resizing, contrast over imagery (4.5:1) and reduced motion. Example opening: a developer asking what happens to cards on a tablet. Takeaway: add a one-page behaviour sheet to every handover and check whether a developer could answer each point unaided.
opening: Open with a concrete moment from everyday work that the reader will recognise.
